summary:
Bangladesh is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The mass uprising that forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina from power in August 2024, known as the Monsoon Revolution, is the inflection point: hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground in its aftermath, and trans people who had been visible in public life withdrew into hiding. A Washington Blade assessment published on 5 August 2025, one year after the ouster, found the country's LGBTQ community increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.

The legal baseline remains the Penal Code 1860, which criminalises intercourse against the order of nature with a penalty of up to life imprisonment. Outright International, whose country profile was updated on 12 March 2026, reports that the provision is rarely prosecuted but is used by police to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (September 2023, updated April 2026) records continuing ambiguity in the scope of the provision, and its application to gender identity is not settled in the material available.

Formal recognition exists alongside this. Bangladesh has recognised a third gender officially since 2013, with the legal framework dating to 2014, and gender-marker change is permitted; hijra pride and LGBTIQ pride events have been held. In 2021 a rural town elected a trans woman as its mayor. Global Press Journal's reporting documents that this recognition has not translated into safety since 2024, with the trans people it profiled now living in hiding.

The current national incident baseline is set by the advocacy group JMBF, whose annual report published in April 2026 documents 260 human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across the country in 2025. JMBF describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend recorded since 2022. The violations include murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion.

Lethal violence against visible trans people continues. Shila, a prominent trans advocate originally from Chattogram district who was widely known for humanitarian work, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025. Five unidentified individuals were accused in the case.

Policing of visibly trans people is frequently extortion-driven. After a group of hijras refused police extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala. On 17 September 2025 police arrested twelve hijras in Narayanganj for collecting money from vehicles carrying expatriates, a traditional hijra livelihood. In April 2024, five trans women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to roughly a month in custody, showing that enforcement reaches transit hubs.

Foreign adjudicators treat the country as unsafe for LGBT people on the evidence. A UK Upper Tribunal decision (PA/07096/2017, February 2019) relied on Home Office country material recording Islamist groups calling for the prosecution of LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues, drawing on fact-finding missions and the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada.
tangentialFactors:
The contrast between legal form and lived practice is the defining feature of the jurisdiction. A decade of official third-gender recognition, an elected trans woman mayor and held pride events coexist with documented hiding, extortion and murder, so a visitor should not read the recognition framework as a safety indicator.

The enforcement pattern is harassment and predation rather than prosecution. The colonial-era sodomy statute is described by Outright International as rarely enforced against a completed case, yet routinely invoked by officers extracting money; the practical exposure for a visible trans visitor is stops, demands and fabricated charges rather than a trial.

Street-level livelihoods are the flashpoint. Money collection from passers-by and vehicles and begging are traditional hijra occupations and are also the activity most consistently policed, which raises exposure for anyone visibly gender-nonconforming near transport nodes and busy roads.

Foreign asylum authorities have independently assessed the country as unsafe, with a UK Upper Tribunal decision and Canadian refugee board material both cited as country evidence, and a UK Home Office policy note still open on key questions of legal scope as of its April 2026 update.
localsOnly:
Residents of the recognised third-gender community carry a legal gender marker that may be changed, a right in place since the 2014 framework, and community pride events have been organised domestically.

Extortion demands from police are a routine operating cost of street livelihoods, and refusal has produced mass injury, as the September 2025 retaliation in Gomdondi Phultala shows. Collecting alms or small payments from passengers and vehicles remains criminalised in practice through arrest, as in Narayanganj.

Documentation and advocacy work carries personal risk. JMBF's reporting tracks a rising violation count year on year since 2022, and a nationally known trans humanitarian worker was killed at her home in Rangamati in February 2025.

Residents report withdrawal from public life since 2024, with previously visible activists living in hiding and community organisations operating under threat from organised Islamist groups.

Unresolved: the sources do not state whether a third-gender marker obtained under domestic law is accepted on passports or at immigration counters, and there is no sourced information on entry screening or visa practice affecting trans travellers specifically.

Unresolved: the outcome of the Shila case is not stated beyond the accusation of five unidentified individuals; no arrests, charges or convictions are recorded in the available material.

Unresolved: the sources do not establish whether the 2014 recognition and gender-marker change procedure remain administered on the same terms after the 2024 change of government, nor whether any restriction has been formally imposed.

Unresolved: the UK Home Office note records unresolved ambiguity over the reach of the colonial-era sodomy provision, including as against female-female activity, and the sources do not settle whether the provision has been applied to trans status or gender identity in any reported conviction.
